subject: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-demo follow-up
messages:
From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acmehealth.com>, Priya Shah <priya.shah@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-15T14:05:00-07:00
Subject: TTFT & streaming SLOs — post-demo follow-up

Hi Alex / Priya,

Thanks again for taking the demo today — really appreciate the time. Quick recap and next steps so we have alignment on the TTFT / streaming requirements you described: 

What we heard from you:
- TTFT target: <= 200 ms (p95) for user-facing streaming responses; ideal target called out during the meeting was 150 ms p95 for typical single-turn responses up to ~256 tokens.
- Streaming: prefer WebSocket for low-latency UX, SSE is also acceptable if WebSocket is blocked. You emphasized first-token latency and smooth chunk cadence (no visible stalls).
- Chunk cadence: goal is visible tokens/partial responses every ~150-250 ms; chunk size ~150–400 characters (roughly 30–80 tokens) works for your UI.
- Throughput / concurrency: expected peak of ~100 concurrent streaming sessions, sustained average ~40–60 concurrent; burst RPS up to ~200 req/s during heavy traffic. Typical session length ~10–20s; avg tokens per response ~200–400.

Our proposed immediate next steps:
1) Can you confirm the numbers above (TTFT p95 target, concurrency, tokens per response) so we lock the SLA baseline?
2) We'll produce a recommended baseline config (model variant, instance sizing, batching/concurrency caps, streaming flush cadence) and a short load-test plan.
3) If you can share existing load-test traces or a sample request set (or allow us to re-run a synthetic workload), we'll run an initial TTFT + streaming cadence test on a dedicated cluster and share results.

Attachments: demo recording (acme_demo_recording.mp4) and a short template for load-test inputs (see Drive link).

CC'ing Marissa and our infra lead to scope the tech follow-up. Looking to schedule the PoC run next week if that works for you.

Best,
Aditya Rao

Aditya — thanks for the clear recap. This aligns closely with what we discussed. A few clarifications from our side: 

- The 150 ms p95 target would be excellent and is what our product team prefers; we can accept up to 200 ms p95 as a contingency. Can your PoC show both p50/p95 for TTFT?
- We will plan for WebSocket streaming; SSE is only a fallback for web clients that don't support websockets.
- Chunk cadence: 200 ms average between chunks is our baseline expectation — occasional spikes of 350–400 ms are OK as long as they are rare.
- Traffic: our initial PoC will simulate 50–80 concurrent streaming users with bursts to 150 concurrent; long-term production could reach the 100 concurrent number you noted.

We'll upload a small request set and a sample UI load profile to the Drive folder by EOD. Also, please include an example config showing how you'll cap batching and concurrency to prioritize TTFT during PoC.

Would like to meet with your engineering/infra folks before the PoC — can we do a 30-min call on Monday 07/18 at 11:00 AM PT? Priya and I will join.

Thanks — Alex
Alex Johnson
Senior Product Manager, Acme Health
alex.johnson@acmehealth.com

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Date: 2028-07-16T09:05:00-07:00
Subject: Fwd: TTFT & streaming SLOs — baseline config + load-test request

Looping in Dev to validate and propose an initial test plan. High-level recommendations for the PoC (based on the numbers above):

- Model & instance: rw-mid-13B (8-bit quantized) on dedicated GPU nodes (A100 equivalent). Pin 2 replicas for initial test; autoscale min_replicas=2, max_replicas=12 depending on throughput.
- Batching & concurrency: target batch size tuned to preserve TTFT — start with batch_size=8 and max_concurrency_per_replica=16 for streaming endpoints. Use synchronous streaming path (continuous flushing) to optimize first-token latency.
- TTFT SLO: aim for p50 ~40–80 ms, p95 <= 150–200 ms for initial cluster config. We'll instrument both cold-start and steady-state.
- Streaming flush policy: recommend flush on either every 50 tokens OR every 150 ms, whichever comes first. This generally keeps chunk cadence sub-200 ms for our tokenization profile.
- Network & endpoint: co-locate PoC in us-west-2; use regional endpoint + peering for best path. Recommend WebSocket for persistent connections; fall back to SSE if needed.
- Observability: capture per-request TTFT, chunk timestamps, token counts, CPU/GPU utilization, and kernel timings. We'll produce a short dashboard for the PoC.

Dev — can you confirm the feasibility and produce a short load-test plan (traffic profile, synthetic payloads, measurement hooks) by Friday 7/17? I'll sync with Aditya to align schedule with Acme's availability (they asked for Mon 7/18 meeting).

Thanks,
Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com

From: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acmehealth.com>, Priya Shah <priya.shah@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-07-17T09:30:00-07:00
Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming SLOs — PoC confirmation and test plan

Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks for the details and for uploading the sample request set. We reviewed the profile and agree the targets are achievable with a dedicated PoC cluster and the configuration below. Summary of the technical plan: 

1) Baseline cluster config (PoC):
   - Model: rw-mid-13B, 8-bit quantized variant (low memory footprint, good latency).
   - Nodes: dedicated GPU nodes (A100 v3 class), initial allocation: 2 replicas pinned for baseline; scale to up to 8 replicas during burst testing.
   - Concurrency caps: max_concurrency_per_replica = 16; global concurrency limit enforced at the route layer to protect TTFT.

2) Streaming behavior and TTFT:
   - First-token: we expect cold p95 in the ~180–220 ms range for a fully cold path; warm p95 ~80–150 ms. With pinning and KV cache warm-up, we should consistently hit <=150 ms p95 for warm conditions.
   - Chunk cadence: implementation will flush every 50 tokens OR every 150 ms (whichever occurs first). In our internal tests that produces chunk intervals typically between 80–200 ms depending on tokenization and response length.
   - WebSocket preferred. We'll provide a sample client script for the PoC showing how to read chunk boundaries and reassemble partial responses.

3) Load-test plan and metrics:
   - Test phases: ramp (0→50 concurrent), steady (50 concurrent for 10 min), burst (150 concurrent for 2 min), long-tail (80 concurrent for 30 min).
   - Metrics captured: TTFT (p50/p95/p99), chunk inter-arrival times, tokens-per-second, GPU utilization, queue latency, kernel execution time.
   - Artifacts: acme_loadtest_summary.csv (sample results), initial_latency_screenshots.png, and raw event traces (available on Drive).

4) Network & client guidance:
   - Use the regional endpoint in us-west-2. TLS handshake adds ~5–15 ms; persistent WebSocket connections avoid repeated handshakes.
   - For mobile clients with variable networks, we recommend an edge-proxy or local batching to smooth jitter.

Next steps:
- We'll run the PoC during the week of 7/18 with Acme's sample load. Can you confirm Monday 7/18 11:00 AM PT for the engineering sync?
- We'll share the PoC report within 48 hours of the test window.

Thanks — looking forward to it.

Best,
Dev Patel
Infra Lead, Redwood Inference
dev_patel@redwood.com
